title: The Burden of Moab
overview: Isaiah 15 pronounces a prophetic oracle against Moab, a neighboring nation east of Israel. The chapter vividly describes the devastation and mourning that will come upon Moab due to divine judgment. Through poetic lamentations, the text portrays the destruction of Moab’s cities, the despair of its people, and the desolation of its land. This chapter serves as a sobering reminder of God’s sovereignty over nations and His righteous judgment against pride and rebellion. Positioned within Isaiah’s larger corpus, this oracle highlights the consequences of opposing God’s purposes and the certainty of His justice extending beyond Israel to the surrounding nations.
structure:
**Verses 1-3: The Initial Destruction and Mourning.** The chapter opens with the announcement of Moab’s ruin during the night, emphasizing the suddenness and completeness of the devastation. The people respond with public mourning, including baldness and sackcloth, traditional signs of grief.

**Verses 4-5: The Widespread Lament and Flight.** The lamentation spreads through Moab’s cities, with cries reaching distant places. The people flee in desperation, symbolized by the reference to Zoar, and the path of their flight is marked by weeping and cries of destruction.

**Verses 6-9: The Desolation of the Land and Final Judgment.** The natural resources of Moab, such as waters and grass, are described as withered and bloodied, symbolizing utter desolation. The chapter concludes with a declaration of intensified judgment, including the imagery of lions preying on survivors, underscoring the completeness of Moab’s downfall.

keyVerses.text: The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence;
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the prophecy against Moab, highlighting the sudden and total destruction of key cities. It sets the tone for the chapter’s theme of divine judgment and the silencing of Moab’s power.

keyVerses.text: He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off.
keyVerses.significance: This verse depicts the intense mourning rituals of Moab’s people, illustrating the depth of their grief and the cultural expressions of sorrow, which emphasize the severity of their calamity.

keyVerses.text: For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing.
keyVerses.significance: Here the natural desolation of Moab’s land symbolizes the comprehensive nature of the judgment. The loss of water and vegetation signifies economic ruin and the cessation of life’s sustenance.

keyVerses.text: For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.
keyVerses.significance: This verse portrays the finality of judgment with vivid imagery of blood and predatory lions, symbolizing divine wrath and the destruction of any survivors, reinforcing God’s sovereign justice.

characters.name: Moab
characters.description: A nation east of Israel, subject of this oracle. Moab’s cities and people face devastation and mourning due to divine judgment for their rebellion and pride.

characters.name: The People of Moab
characters.description: The inhabitants who respond to the destruction with lamentation, sackcloth, and baldness, demonstrating their grief and recognition of impending doom.

characters.name: God
characters.description: Though not directly speaking in this chapter, God is the sovereign judge whose judgment brings about Moab’s ruin, demonstrating His authority over nations.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes God’s righteous judgment on Moab for its sins, illustrating that no nation is beyond His authority and justice.
The vivid descriptions of grief rituals highlight the human response to divine judgment and loss, connecting to biblical traditions of repentance and sorrow.
The imagery of withered land and blood-filled waters symbolizes total devastation, reflecting the consequences of turning away from God.

historicalContext: Isaiah 15 was written during the 8th century BC, a time when the kingdom of Judah faced threats from expanding empires such as Assyria. Moab, located east of the Dead Sea in modern-day Jordan, was a frequent adversary of Israel and Judah. The cities mentioned—Ar, Kir, Bajith, Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar, Luhith, Horonaim, Nimrim, Eglaim, Beerelim, and Dimon—were key Moabite centers. The cultural customs of mourning, including cutting hair and wearing sackcloth, were common expressions of grief in the ancient Near East. Politically, Moab’s alliances and conflicts with Israel and Judah often led to divine pronouncements of judgment through prophets like Isaiah.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective sees Isaiah 15 as a clear demonstration of God’s sovereign justice over all nations, emphasizing that God’s wrath is executed righteously against sin and rebellion, serving as a warning to all peoples.

Dispensational interpreters view this oracle as part of God’s prophetic timeline concerning the nations surrounding Israel, highlighting the specific historical judgment on Moab while anticipating future restoration of Israel.
Early church commentators often interpreted Moab’s judgment typologically, seeing it as a foreshadowing of the judgment awaiting all who oppose God, while also emphasizing the call to repentance.

crossReferences.connection: Another extensive prophecy against Moab, affirming the theme of divine judgment and desolation found in Isaiah 15.
Ezekiel also pronounces judgment on Moab, reinforcing the consistent biblical message of accountability for nations opposing God.
Amos declares God’s judgment on Moab for their transgressions, paralleling Isaiah’s oracle in highlighting Moab’s sin and punishment.
Describes mourning customs similar to those in Isaiah 15, such as cutting hair and wearing sackcloth, underscoring biblical expressions of grief.
Speaks of bloodshed and desolation, echoing the imagery of blood-filled waters and destruction in Isaiah 15.

application: Recognize God’s sovereignty over all nations and submit to His righteous authority in your life.
Respond to God’s discipline with genuine mourning and repentance rather than resistance.
Trust in God’s justice when facing the consequences of sin, knowing He will ultimately make all things right.
Cultivate a heart of compassion and prayer for those under judgment, like Moab’s people lamenting their fate.
Remember that desolation results from turning away from God, so pursue obedience and faithfulness daily.
conclusion: Isaiah 15 powerfully reminds believers that God’s justice extends beyond Israel to all nations, including Moab, whose destruction and mourning serve as a solemn warning. The chapter’s vivid imagery of desolation and lamentation calls Christians to recognize God’s sovereign authority, respond to His discipline with repentance, and trust in His righteous judgment. By reflecting on Moab’s fate, believers are encouraged to live faithfully under God’s rule, embracing humility and obedience as safeguards against divine judgment.
timeline: c. 740-700 BC - Prophecies of Isaiah during the reign of King Hezekiah in Judah

definitions.definition: A prophetic oracle or message, often of judgment, that a prophet carries and delivers from God.
In biblical mourning customs, shaving the head as a sign of grief and repentance.
A coarse garment worn during times of mourning or penitence to express sorrow.
A young female cow; here used symbolically to represent the city of Zoar.

outline.heading: The Destruction of Moab’s Cities
outline.description: Announces the sudden ruin of Moab’s key cities and depicts the profound mourning of its people through traditional signs of grief.

outline.heading: The Spread of Lamentation and Flight
outline.description: Describes the widespread cries of sorrow across Moab and the desperate flight of its inhabitants seeking refuge.

outline.heading: The Desolation of the Land and Final Judgment
outline.description: Portrays the natural devastation of Moab’s environment and the intensified divine judgment symbolized by bloodied waters and predatory lions.
